The second skipped a lecture because large classes feel tedious and online materials are convenient, but agrees to attend and participate in future. The third prefers small seminars but points out that large lectures can still offer face-to-face interaction and teach many students at once.

title: On-campus vs Off-campus Accommodation
narration: Three students are talking about their living experiences in on-campus dorms and off-campus housing.
turns: Speaker 1

I live in a house off campus with my friends. It's quite far from the school, but I am lucky because I live close to bus stops and it is very convenient. Also, our landlord is nice and takes care of things like cleaning and other problems around the house.
Speaker 2

I live in the school dormitory, which is very convenient, and there are places where I can study. Also, I don't want to get up early, and the dormitory is very close to the teaching buildings. Actually, I'd be quite happy to share a house with friends off campus, but the rent is too expensive.
Speaker 3

I also live in the school dormitory. If anything in the dorm breaks, it gets repaired soon, so students don't have to bother with it. Some friends living outside have problems with water and have to wait for a long time to have it fixed.
Speaker 1

That's honestly a huge advantage of living on campus. Even though our landlord is responsible and helpful, off-campus maintenance is really slow in general. We once had a water leakage issue and waited nearly a week for someone to fix it, which was really troublesome.
Speaker 2

While dorm life has plenty of benefits, it definitely comes with some annoying downsides as well. My roommate often gets up as early as 5 a.m., and the noise she makes when getting up seriously disrupts my sleep.
Speaker 3

Yes, living in the dorm really has downsides. The fire alarm in our dormitory building often goes off in the middle of the night. Whenever the alarm goes off, we have to leave the building and wait until it has been checked. I'm fed up with being forced to get out of bed and evacuate outside because of fire alarms on cold winter nights because I've experienced twice. Both times they were caused by illegal use of a toaster in the building. Can't they find the people who are cooking illegally and deal with them more quickly? Still, I think the system is quite safe, so I accept this accommodation plan.
Speaker 1

I had no idea dorm life had such annoying safety issues. Living off-campus definitely gives us more private space and flexible schedules. We can cook freely in our own kitchen without violating any campus rules, and we never suffer from sudden fire alarms at night.
Speaker 2

That sounds really relaxing, but off-campus accommodation still has obvious drawbacks. Apart from the high rent and slow maintenance, you also have to spend plenty of time on daily housework and commuting every single day.
Speaker 3

Exactly. Every living option has its own pros and cons. On-campus dorms are affordable, safe and time-saving, while off-campus houses provide more freedom and privacy. It all depends on personal study habits and lifestyle choices.
facts: The students compare on-campus dorms and off-campus housing.
The first appreciates the privacy and flexibility of sharing an off-campus house, although maintenance can take longer.
The second likes the convenience of the dorm but mentions an early-rising roommate and notes the costs and chores of living off campus.
The third values quick dorm repairs but dislikes overnight fire alarms. They conclude that the choice depends on study habits and lifestyle.
sample: The students compare on-campus dorms and off-campus housing. The first appreciates the privacy and flexibility of sharing an off-campus house, although maintenance can take longer. The second likes the convenience of the dorm but mentions an early-rising roommate and notes the costs and chores of living off campus. The third values quick dorm repairs but dislikes overnight fire alarms. They conclude that the choice depends on study habits and lifestyle.

title: Library Rules
narration: Two students and one librarian are having a discussion in the library, focusing on the noise problem, rule enforcement and suggestions for improving the learning environment.
turns: Speaker 1

The library is supposed to be a quiet, peaceful place for people to focus on their studies, finish assignments, or prepare for exams. But recently, many students in the library have been talking loudly, laughing, and even chatting freely with their friends, making it feel more like a busy social club than a place for academic work.
Speaker 2

I am well aware of this situation, and I completely understand your frustration. However, their noisy behavior is quite difficult for us to manage effectively. As you can see, our library is quite large, with multiple floors, reading areas, and public spaces, and we simply do not have enough staff to monitor every corner and every student's behavior at all times. Perhaps you could consider moving to the first floor or the computer area, where the atmosphere is a bit more relaxed.
Speaker 3

Unfortunately, the computer area isn't any better. Many students there watch sports games, entertainment videos, or even live streams on their computers, and they often play the audio very loudly without using headphones. On top of that, their conversations are also quite noisy. All this noise makes it just as hard for us to concentrate on our work as the main reading area, if not harder.
Speaker 1

I see what you mean. Maybe a clearer division of areas would help. Perhaps it would be more effective to clearly state the rules. For example, small talking should be allowed in the computer area. Meanwhile, in the main reading area and silent study rooms, people should try not to talk at all, not even in a low voice. This way, students will know exactly where it is acceptable to talk.
Speaker 2
Actually, talking is already allowed in our computer area. As for the silent area, if you ever feel distracted by noise there, you can call the security desk directly for help.
Speaker 1
I think the library should strengthen its promotion of these rules.
Speaker 2
That's a very good suggestion. You'd better write down your complaints and suggestions in detail. The university attaches great importance to students’ opinions.
Speaker 3

That's good to know, but why do some people bring drinks into the library? Is that permitted? I've seen students spill their drinks on the tables and chairs several times, leaving stains that are hard to clean.
Speaker 2

Bringing drinks into the library is actually not allowed. Drinks can easily be spilled, making the library environment messy and untidy, and they can also cause damage to books, tables, and other public facilities.
facts: Two students and a librarian discuss noise and other rules in the library.
The first student proposes clearer divisions between quiet and shared spaces and better publicity for the rules.
The librarian explains that talking is allowed in the computer area, says students can report noise in the silent area, and invites written feedback.
The other student mentions computer noise and spilled drinks. The librarian explains that drinks are prohibited because spills can damage facilities and books.
sample: Two students and a librarian discuss noise and other rules in the library. The first student proposes clearer divisions between quiet and shared spaces and better publicity for the rules. The librarian explains that talking is allowed in the computer area, says students can report noise in the silent area, and invites written feedback. The other student mentions computer noise and spilled drinks. The librarian explains that drinks are prohibited because spills can damage facilities and books.

title: Lectures and Tutorials
narration: Three students are discussing different types of classes at university.
turns: Speaker 1

There are no lectures in high school, so coming to university and adapting to new class forms has been quite a big change for me. Most of the classes at university are large lectures, and honestly, I find the effectiveness of a lecture depends on who gives it. Some teachers speak extremely fast during the lecture, and a few of them have strong accents, which makes it even harder for me to understand every knowledge point and detailed content they explain in class.
Speaker 2

Personally, I have a different opinion and I quite like university lectures. One obvious advantage is that teachers will timely upload their PowerPoint slides and course materials online after class. So even if you miss a lecture or fail to catch every single detail during class, you can always review the complete slides and supplement your knowledge later. However, I still think small-group tutorials have their unique advantages that lectures cannot replace.
Speaker 3

I totally agree with you that tutorials are much better in many ways, and I don't really like long lectures either. University lectures are simply too long and tiring for students. Sometimes a single lecture lasts for a full hour, and some even extend to ninety minutes straight. It is really challenging to stay focused and concentrate on only one person speaking for such a long period of time without any interaction.
Speaker 1

That's exactly how I feel. Long lectures always make me feel distracted and exhausted. I strongly prefer tutorial classes, just like you mentioned. Tutorials are usually small-sized and highly interactive, so it's much easier for us to get targeted help whenever we encounter confusing knowledge points.
Speaker 2

That's the biggest highlight of tutorials. The small class atmosphere allows students to communicate freely with tutors and classmates. Unlike large lectures where hundreds of students sit in one hall and hardly have a chance to interact, tutorials enable us to have in-depth discussions and share different learning ideas.
Speaker 3

I've had really positive learning experiences in all my tutorial classes so far. Most of the tutors I've met are very patient and responsible. They will carefully explain confusing knowledge points repeatedly and provide extra learning guidance for students who fall behind.
Speaker 1

Absolutely. I feel that lectures are more suitable for us to systematically learn basic theoretical knowledge in a short time. But when it comes to digesting difficult content and solving personal learning problems, tutorials are absolutely irreplaceable for university students.
Speaker 2

That makes perfect sense. These two class forms have their own strengths. Lectures ensure the overall learning progress of all students, while tutorials make up for the lack of interaction and personalized teaching in large public classes.
Speaker 3
I totally agree with this view. Combining lectures and tutorials perfectly is the best way for us to adapt to university study and improve our academic performance steadily.
facts: The students compare university lectures and tutorials.
The first finds fast speech and accents hard to follow and prefers tutorials for discussion, while valuing lectures for foundational theory.
The second appreciates that lecture materials are uploaded and says small tutorials make it easier to ask questions and interact.
The third finds long lectures tiring and values the individual help tutors provide. They agree that lectures and tutorials complement each other.
sample: The students compare university lectures and tutorials. The first finds fast speech and accents hard to follow and prefers tutorials for discussion, while valuing lectures for foundational theory. The second appreciates that lecture materials are uploaded and says small tutorials make it easier to ask questions and interact. The third finds long lectures tiring and values the individual help tutors provide. They agree that lectures and tutorials complement each other.

title: Study Places
narration: three students are discussing where they should study.
turns: Speaker 1
Let's go to the library to study. I think it helps me get into the study mood quickly. Home is full of little things that pull my attention away. I really need a quiet space for my homework.
Speaker 2

I prefer studying at home because I can eat snacks whenever I want and stay in my pajamas. I do not like following strict rules in public areas. I can also take short breaks whenever I feel tired. It is the most comfortable choice for me.
Speaker 3

When at home, I always want to do housework. I have no motivation during the day, but I feel really motivated at night. However, by then, it's too late to go to the library, because seats are hard to get. Some people leave their belongings on chairs to reserve seats.
Speaker 1

I often get distracted by my phone at home, and sometimes my younger sister plays music really loudly, so I can't concentrate on studying. I would still take my laptop to the library, even though I can also waste time browsing distracting social media on it. Seeing everyone else studying there might make me feel some pressure. Since I've come all the way here, I might as well focus on studying.
Speaker 2

You're assuming that everyone goes to the library to study, but whenever I go there, people are chatting, such as holding group discussions. The lower floors of the library tend to be quite noisy. The upper floors, especially the third floor, have separate study rooms that you can book in advance. Those rooms are much better for quiet work.
Speaker 3

By the way, we can also lock our phones in the lockers near the library entrance. This simple trick can stop most phone distractions. It works well for people who easily scroll online. Maybe we can try this method together later.
Speaker 1
That locker idea sounds really useful to me. I often pick up my phone without thinking. A locked phone will force me to stay on task. I am willing to give it a try today.
Speaker 2
There are classrooms in our department where we can study, but that's a secret, so don't tell anyone. We can study there. It is usually empty and much quieter. No one will come to disturb us inside.
Speaker 3
I'll go with you. This secret spot sounds better than fighting for library seats. I don't want to race others to grab seats late at night. Let's keep this place to ourselves.
facts: The students discuss where they can concentrate on studying.
The first prefers the library because of distractions at home and is willing to lock away their phone.
The second finds studying at home more comfortable, points out that the library can be noisy and suggests a quiet departmental classroom.
The third struggles to work at home, recommends library phone lockers and agrees to try the classroom rather than compete for a library seat.

The second finds studying at home more comfortable, points out that the library can be noisy and suggests a quiet departmental classroom. The third struggles to work at home, recommends library phone lockers and agrees to try the classroom rather than compete for a library seat.
